claims.text: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy, such as an Nb–Mo–Ta–W-family alloy, will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition with increasing temperature.
A complex, distorted lattice enables the proposed refractory alloy to resist conventional temper embrittlement.
A hierarchical microstructure enables the proposed refractory alloy to resist conventional temper embrittlement.
Interface decohesion or activation of less-mobile phases can temporarily reduce ductility in an intermediate temperature range.
Activation of additional slip systems and diffusion-aided deformation restores ductility at higher temperatures.
The processed refractory alloy has a hierarchical two-phase or dual-lamella microstructure.
The processed refractory alloy is predominantly ductile at low temperature.
Using an inert atmosphere or vacuum avoids oxidation during the temperature ramp.
Slow temperature changes permit microstructural evolution during the experiment.
The alloy contains a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces.
Multiple principal refractory elements produce a distribution of local lattice distortions.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity predominates at low temperature.
Intermediate-temperature interface decohesion or activation of less-mobile phases produces a brittle response similar to temper embrittlement.
At high temperature, additional slip systems and enhanced atomic diffusion reintroduce ductility.
The alloy will have high low-temperature ductility, a pronounced ductility drop in a narrow intermediate window, and recovered high-temperature ductility.
The transition depends on alloy composition and processing history.
Significant alteration of phase distribution or interface coherency may eliminate the transition.
